about.text: Robert Smythson was an English architect. Smythson designed a number of notable houses during the Elizabethan era. Little is known about his birth and upbringing—his first mention in historical records comes in 1556, when he was stonemason for the house at Longleat, built by Sir John Thynne.
about.title: Robert Smythson

about.text: Sir Robert Taylor was an English architect and sculptor who worked in London and the south of England.
about.title: Robert Taylor (architect)

about.text: John Carr was an English architect. He is best known for Buxton Crescent in Derbyshire and Harewood House in West Yorkshire. Much of his work was in the Palladian style.
about.title: John Carr (architect)

about.text: James Gandon was an English architect best known for his work in Ireland during the late 18th and early 19th centuries. His best known works include the Custom House, Beresford Place, Four Courts and King's Inns in Dublin and Emo Court in County Laois.
about.title: James Gandon

about.text: William Stretton was a builder and architect based in Nottingham.
about.title: William Stretton

about.text: Sir Jeffry Wyatville was an English architect and garden designer. Born Jeffry Wyatt into an established dynasty of architects, in 1824 he was allowed by King George IV to change his surname to Wyatville. He is mainly remembered for making alterations and extensions to Chatsworth House and Windsor Castle.
about.title: Jeffry Wyatville

about.text: Peter Frederick Robinson was an English architect.
about.title: Peter Frederick Robinson

about.text: Thomas Rickman was an English architect and architectural antiquary who was a major figure in the Gothic Revival. He is particularly remembered for his Attempt to Discriminate the Styles of English Architecture, which established the basic chronological classification and terminology that are still in widespread use for the different styles of English medieval ecclesiastical architecture.
about.title: Thomas Rickman

about.text: Edward James Willson was an English architect, antiquary, architectural writer, and mayor of Lincoln in 1851–2.
about.title: Edward James Willson

about.text: Thomas Oliver was an English classical architect and surveyor active in Newcastle upon Tyne. He was one of the numerous local architects who worked with Richard Grainger on the development of Newcastle, but his work tends to be overshadowed by that of John Dobson, who has been given a great deal of the credit for the central part of the city referred to as Grainger Town.
about.title: Thomas Oliver (architect)

about.text: Charles Blacker Vignoles was an Irish railway engineer, and eponym of the Vignoles rail.
about.title: Charles Blacker Vignoles

about.text: Captain Gilbert Smith Doughty CE was an architect based in Nottingham and Matlock.

about.text: Henry Isaac Stevens FRIBA was an architect based in Derby. He was born in London, in 1806, and died in 1873. In the late 1850s he changed his name to Isaac Henry Stevens.
about.title: Henry Isaac Stevens

about.text: John Johnson was an English architect who specialised in religious buildings and churches in the Gothic style. He was regularly employed by the civil engineer Sir John Kelk to design the homes and public buildings Kelk funded.
about.title: John Johnson (architect, born 1807)

about.text: Samuel Sutton Rawlinson was an architect and engineer known for his work in Nottingham.
about.title: Samuel Sutton Rawlinson

about.text: Sir George Gilbert Scott, largely known as Sir Gilbert Scott, was a prolific English Gothic Revival architect, chiefly associated with the design, building and renovation of churches and cathedrals, although he started his career as a leading designer of workhouses. Over 800 buildings were designed or altered by him.
about.title: George Gilbert Scott

about.text: Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin was an English architect, designer, artist and critic with French and Swiss origins. He is principally remembered for his pioneering role in the Gothic Revival style of architecture. Among his best-known work is the interior of the Palace of Westminster and its clock tower nicknamed 'Big Ben'.
about.title: Augustus Pugin

about.text: Thomas Simpson was an English architect based in Nottingham.

about.text: John Loughborough Pearson was a British Gothic Revival architect renowned for his work on churches and cathedrals. Pearson revived and practised largely the art of vaulting, and acquired in it a proficiency unrivalled in his generation. He worked on at least 210 ecclesiastical buildings in England alone in a career spanning 54 years.
about.title: John Loughborough Pearson

about.text: James Huckerby was a 19th-century builder and architect based in Beeston, Nottingham.

about.title: George Frederick Bodley

about.text: Alfred Waterhouse was an English architect, particularly associated with Gothic Revival architecture, although he designed using other architectural styles as well. He is perhaps best known for his designs for Manchester Town Hall and the Natural History Museum in London. He designed other town halls, the Manchester Assize buildings—bombed in World War II—and the adjacent Strangeways Prison.
about.title: Alfred Waterhouse

about.text: William Arthur Heazell FRIBA was an architect based in Nottingham.

about.text: Robert Evans FRIBA, JP was an English architect based in Nottingham.

about.text: Richard Charles Sutton was an architect based in Nottingham. He was born 1834 and died on 18 October 1915. He was a member of Nottingham City Council from 1887 to 1901.
about.title: Richard Charles Sutton

about.text: Marriott Ogle Tarbotton MICE, FGS, FRMS, was born in Leeds on 6 December 1834 and died in Nottingham on 6 March 1887. He was Borough Engineer for Nottingham from 1859.
about.title: Marriott Ogle Tarbotton

about.text: Charles John Phipps was an English architect known for more than forty theatres he designed in the latter half of the nineteenth century. He began his own practice in his native Bath in 1857, designing buildings and furniture in the Gothic Revival style. In 1862 he gained his first theatre commission, the Theatre Royal, Bath, which generally retaining the Georgian character of the original theatre on the site.
about.title: C. J. Phipps

about.text: Thomas Verity was an English theatre architect during the theatre-building boom of 1885–1915. Verity began his career articled in the architecture department of the War Office, assisting in the erection of the South Kensington Museum. He further assisted in the building of the Royal Albert Hall between 1867 and 1870.
about.title: Thomas Verity

about.text: Charles Trubshaw FRIBA was an architect specifically associated with railway buildings on the London and North Western Railway and Midland Railway lines.
about.title: Charles Trubshaw

about.title: John Collyer

about.text: Watson Fothergill was a British architect who designed over 100 unique buildings in Nottingham in the East Midlands of England. His influences were mainly from the Gothic Revival and Old English vernacular architecture styles. His work dates from 1864 to around 1912.
about.title: Watson Fothergill

about.text: Francis Matcham was an English architect who specialised in the design of theatres and music halls. He worked extensively in London, predominantly under Moss Empires for whom he designed the Hippodrome in 1900, Hackney Empire, Shepherd's Bush Empire, Coliseum, and Palladium. His last major commission before retirement was the Victoria Palace Theatre in 1911 for the variety magnate Alfred Butt.

about.text: Thomas Cecil Howitt, OBE was a British provincial architect of the 20th Century. Howitt is chiefly remembered for designing prominent public buildings, such as the Council House and Processional Way in Nottingham, Baskerville House in Birmingham, Newport Civic Centre, and several Odeon cinemas. Howitt's chief architectural legacies are in his home city of Nottingham.

Howitt is chiefly remembered for designing prominent public buildings, such as the Council House and Processional Way in Nottingham, Baskerville House in Birmingham, Newport Civic Centre, and several Odeon cinemas. Howitt's chief architectural legacies are in his home city of Nottingham.

about.text: George Brough was a motorcycle racer and a world record–holding motorcycle and automobile manufacturer and showman. He was known for his powerful and expensive Brough Superior motorcycles which were the first superbikes. George died in 1970 but his legacy lives on in the many Brough Superior motorcycles maintained by enthusiasts to this day.
about.title: George Brough

about.text: Sir Evan Owen Williams was a British engineer and architect, known for being the principal engineer for the original Wembley Stadium, and later Gravelly Hill Interchange as well as a number of key modernist buildings, including the Express Building in Manchester and the D10 and D6 Buildings at the Boots Factory Site in Nottingham.
about.title: Owen Williams (engineer)

about.text: Peter Meinhard Moro was a London-based architect whose practice developed many notable public buildings. He was the son of Slovenian physician and paediatrician Ernst Moro.
about.title: Peter Moro

about.text: Gerard Thomas Goalen was a British architect who specialised in church architecture and was influenced by continental models and the Liturgical Movement. He was one of the most important architects of the Catholic Modernist movement in the United Kingdom during the 20th century.
about.title: Gerard Goalen

about.text: Emanuel Vincent Harris, often known as E. Vincent Harris, was an English architect who designed several important public buildings in traditional styles.
about.title: E. Vincent Harris

about.text: RHWL Architects was a British architecture practice based in London, Berlin and Qatar. It was created by Andrew Renton, Peter Howard and Humphrey Wood following the establishment of Andrew Renton & Associates in 1961. Gerald Levin became a Name Partner in 1973, and from that date the Firm was often known as 'RHWL'.
about.title: RHWL

about.text: Caruso St John is a British architectural practice founded in 1990 by Adam Caruso and Peter St John. The firm first came to wider attention with The New Art Gallery Walsall, completed after an international competition win in 1995, and has since worked across a broad range of public and private projects. Caruso St John won the RIBA Stirling Prize in 2016 for Newport Street Gallery, having previously been shortlisted in 2000 and 2006.
about.title: Caruso St John

about.text: Gilbert Wakefield was an English scholar and controversialist. He moved from being a cleric and academic, into tutoring at dissenting academies, and finally became a professional writer and publicist. In a celebrated state trial, he was imprisoned for a pamphlet critical of government policy of the French Revolutionary Wars; and died shortly after his release.
about.title: Gilbert Wakefield

about.text: Henry Kirke White was an English poet and hymn-writer. He died at the young age of 21.
about.title: Henry Kirke White

about.text: George Noel Gordon Byron, 6th Baron Byron, known as Lord Byron was a British poet. He was one of the major figures of the Romantic movement, and is regarded as being among the greatest British poets. Among his best known works are the lengthy narratives Don Juan and Childe Harold's Pilgrimage; many of his shorter lyrics in Hebrew Melodies also became popular.
about.title: Lord Byron

about.text: Philip James Bailey was an English poet, best known as the author of Festus.
about.title: Philip James Bailey

about.text: Sir James Matthew Barrie, 1st Baronet was a Scottish novelist and playwright. He was born and educated in Scotland and then moved to London, where he wrote several successful novels and plays.
about.title: J. M. Barrie

about.text: Arthur Henry Mee was an English writer, journalist and educator. He is best known for The Harmsworth Self-Educator, The Children's Encyclopædia, The Children's Newspaper, and The King's England.
about.title: Arthur Mee

about.text: David Herbert Lawrence was an English novelist, short story writer, poet, playwright, literary critic, travel writer, essayist, and painter. His modernist works reflect on modernity, social alienation and industrialisation, while championing sexuality, vitality and instinct.
about.title: D. H. Lawrence

about.text: Henry Graham Greene was an English writer and journalist regarded by many as one of the leading novelists of the 20th century. Combining literary acclaim with widespread popularity, Greene acquired a reputation early in his lifetime as a major writer, both of serious Catholic novels, and of thrillers. He was shortlisted for the Nobel Prize in Literature several times.
about.title: Graham Greene

about.text: George Green was a British mathematical physicist born in Sneinton, Nottinghamshire, now part of the city of Nottingham. Despite receiving little recognition during his lifetime, he is best remembered for his Essay on electricity and magnetism published in 1828.
about.title: George Green (mathematician)

about.text: Edward Joseph Lowe FRS FGS FRAS FLS was a British botanist, meteorologist and astronomer, who published papers on a wide variety of subjects, including luminous meteors, sunspots, the zodiacal light, meteorological observations during the 1860 solar eclipse, conchology, ferns, grasses and other plants.
about.title: Edward Joseph Lowe

about.text: Mary Patricia Kendrick MBE born Mary Patricia Boak was a British tidal engineer who was an expert on silt. She worked on many projects but she is known for leading a team working on the Thames Barrier. She broke a 200 year long list of Admirals who looked after keeping the River Mersey navigable when she appointed Acting Conservator of the River Mersey - a role that dates back to 1625.
about.title: Mary Kendrick

about.text: George John Scipio Africanus was a West African former slave who became a successful entrepreneur in Nottingham, England.
about.title: George Africanus

about.text: Thomas Adams was a British lace manufacturer and philanthropist based in Nottingham.
about.title: Thomas Adams (manufacturer and philanthropist)

about.text: John Levers was an English mechanic and engineer, best known for improving John Heathcoat’s pioneering lace machine; the Leavers machine laid the foundation of the machine lace trade.
about.title: John Levers

about.text: Thomas Humber was an English engineer and cycle manufacturer who developed and patented a safety bicycle with a diamond-shaped frame and wheels of similar size. It became a pattern for subsequent machines. Humber made many other improvements to bicycles.
about.title: Thomas Humber

about.text: Jesse Boot, 1st Baron Trent transformed The Boots Company, founded by his father, John Boot, into a national retailer, which branded itself as "Chemists to the Nation".
about.title: Jesse Boot, 1st Baron Trent

about.text: John Player & Sons, most often known simply as Player's, was a tobacco and cigarette manufacturer based in Nottingham, England. In 1901 the company merged with twelve other companies to become a branch of the Imperial Tobacco Company of Great Britain and Ireland. The company pioneered the advertising with trading cards.
about.title: John Player & Sons

about.text: William Abednego Thompson, also known as Bendigo Thompson and mononymously as Bendigo, was an English bare-knuckle boxer who won the heavyweight championship of England from James Burke on 12 February 1839. He was inducted into The Ring magazine Hall of Fame in 1955, the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1991 and the Bare Knuckle Boxing Hall of Fame in 2011. His nickname of "Bendigo" lives on in the name of a city and creek in Australia.
about.title: William Thompson (boxer)

about.text: His Honour Tinsley Lindley, OBE was an English footballer. He was described as "an ideal centre forward". He scored three goals in his debut aged 16 for Nottingham Forest.
about.title: Tinsley Lindley

about.text: Herbert Kilpin was an English football player and manager, best known as the main founding father of AC Milan. After playing as an amateur in his native city of Nottingham, in the early 1890s he moved to Italy to work in the textile industry and he became one of the pioneers of football in the country, first as a player for Internazionale Torino and then as player, manager, and charter member of Milan.
about.title: Herbert Kilpin

about.text: Albert Iremonger was a football goalkeeper, county-class cricketer and brother of sportsmen Harry Iremonger and James Iremonger.
about.title: Albert Iremonger

about.text: Brian Howard Clough was an English football player and manager, primarily known for his successes as a manager with Derby County and Nottingham Forest. He won the European Cup twice with Nottingham Forest and is one of four managers to have won the English league with two different clubs. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest managers of all time.
about.title: Brian Clough

about.text: Torvill and Dean are British ice dancers and former British, European, Olympic, and World champions. At the Sarajevo 1984 Winter Olympics the pair won gold and became the highest-scoring figure skaters of all time for a single programme, receiving twelve perfect 6.0s and six 5.9s which included artistic impression scores of 6.0 from every judge, after skating to Maurice Ravel's Boléro.
about.title: Torvill and Dean

about.text: William Frederick "W.F." Wallett was a popular circus clown in Victorian England, who also enjoyed modest celebrity in the United States. After he performed before Queen Victoria in 1844 at Windsor Castle, Wallett began promoting himself as "the Queen's Jester", and described himself this way in the title of his 1870 autobiography. For many years, he performed in the circus owned by his good friend Pablo Fanque Wallett also helped manage Fanque's circus.
about.title: W. F. Wallett

about.text: Henry Dawson was a British landscape painter. Born in Kingston upon Hull, Dawson went with his parents to Nottingham when he was still an infant and always regarded the latter as his native town. His parents were poor, and he began life in a Nottingham lace factory.
about.title: Henry Dawson (artist)

about.text: Samuel Bourne was a British photographer known for his prolific seven years' work in India, from 1863 to 1870. Together with Charles Shepherd, he set up Bourne & Shepherd first in Shimla in 1863 and later in Kolkata; the company closed in June 2016.
about.title: Samuel Bourne

about.text: Dame Laura Knight was an English artist who worked in oils, watercolours, etching, engraving and drypoint. Knight was a painter in the figurative, realist tradition, who embraced English Impressionism. In her long career, Knight was among the most successful and popular painters in Britain.
about.title: Laura Knight

about.text: Frank Robinson was an eccentric street entertainer in Nottingham, England. He was by far Nottingham's best known busker and was regularly seen around Nottingham City Centre for over fifteen years. His favourite busking place was outside of the C&A store in the Lister Gate area of the city.
about.title: Frank Robinson (Xylophone Man)

about.text: Richard Arthur Beckinsale was an English actor. He played Lennie Godber in the BBC sitcoms Porridge and Going Straight, and Alan Moore in the ITV sitcom Rising Damp. He was the father of actresses Samantha and Kate Beckinsale.
about.title: Richard Beckinsale

about.text: John Wesley was an English cleric, theologian, and evangelist who was a principal leader of a revival movement within the Church of England known as Methodism. The societies he founded became the dominant form of the ongoing independent Methodist movement. Educated at Charterhouse and Christ Church, Oxford, Wesley was elected a fellow of Lincoln College, Oxford, in 1726 and ordained as an Anglican priest two years later.
about.title: John Wesley

about.text: William Booth was an English Methodist preacher who, along with his wife, Catherine, founded the Salvation Army and became its first General. This Christian movement, founded in 1865, has a quasi-military structure and government and has spread from London to many parts of the world. It is one of the largest distributors of humanitarian aid.
about.title: William Booth

about.text: John Clifford was a British Baptist Nonconformist minister and politician, who became famous as the advocate of passive resistance to the Education Act 1902.
about.title: John Clifford (minister)

about.text: Camille d'Hostun de la Baume, duc de Tallard was a French nobleman, diplomat and military commander, who became a Marshal of France.
about.title: Camille d'Hostun, duc de Tallard

about.text: Admiral of the White Sir John Borlase Warren, 1st Baronet was a Royal Navy officer, diplomat and politician who sat in the British House of Commons between 1774 and 1807.
about.title: John Borlase Warren

about.text: Albert Ball, was a British fighter pilot during the First World War. At the time of his death he was the United Kingdom's leading flying ace, with 44 victories, and remained its fourth-highest scorer behind Edward Mannock, James McCudden and George McElroy. Born and raised in Nottingham, Ball joined the Sherwood Foresters at the outbreak of the First World War and was commissioned as a second lieutenant in October 1914.
about.title: Albert Ball

about.text: Charles I was King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from 27 March 1625 until his execution in 1649. Charles was born into the House of Stuart as the second son of King James VI of Scotland. After his father inherited the English throne in 1603, he moved to England, where he spent much of the rest of his life.
about.title: Charles I of England

about.text: William Ewart Gladstone was a British statesman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom for four non-consecutive terms between 1868 and 1894, the most of any British prime minister. He began in politics as a Conservative Member of Parliament for Newark and ended as the face of the Liberal Party.
about.title: William Ewart Gladstone

about.text: PC Gerald Michael "Ged" Walker was an English police dog handler with Nottinghamshire Police who was killed in the line of duty in Bulwell, Nottingham, in 2003. On 7 January 2003, PC Walker was dragged 100 yards and fatally injured by a stolen taxi as he reached into the vehicle in an attempt to remove the keys from the ignition. He died in hospital two days later from serious head injuries.
about.title: Death of Ged Walker

about.text: Dorothea Nancy Waddingham was an English nursing home matron who was convicted of murder.
about.title: Dorothea Waddingham

links.text: Claims to date from 1189, a date that rests on tradition rather than records. It is built against the castle rock, with rooms cut into the sandstone.
Another claimant to the title of the city's oldest pub. The core of the building dates from around 1360, and unusually large caves lie beneath it.
Claims to be the oldest pub in the city. Tree-ring dating of its timbers suggests it was built around 1420, and its cellars are cut into the sandstone.
One of the three medieval parish churches of Nottingham. Parts of the building date from about 1180.
One of the three medieval parish churches of Nottingham, on a site mentioned in the Domesday Book.
The medieval church was pulled down during the Civil War; the brick church standing today was finished in 1678.
The Catholic cathedral, designed by Augustus Pugin and built between 1841 and 1844.

Built in 1876 to designs by Stuart Colman for a congregation that goes back to 1690 and became Unitarian in 1802. Worship ended in 1982; the chapel then housed a lace museum and is now a Pitcher & Piano.
A medieval timber-framed building, moved to its present site on Castle Road.
A lace showroom and warehouse built for Thomas Adams to a design by Thomas Chambers Hine, opened in 1855.
A shopping centre opened in 1972 on the site of Nottingham Victoria railway station, whose clock tower still stands beside it.

When the House of Lords threw out the Second Reform Bill on 8 October 1831, rioting broke out in Nottingham and a crowd burned the castle, which belonged to the Duke of Newcastle, an opponent of reform. Three men were hanged; the Duke refused to restore the castle, and its burnt shell stood on the rock for years.
The county courthouse and gaol, rebuilt to a design by James Gandon. It is now the National Justice Museum.
The Victorian Guildhall, completed in 1888, held the city's courts and police station.
The station building of red brick and terracotta opened in 1904.
One of the largest paved squares in the United Kingdom. The two towns were once divided by a wall across it, whose line a stainless steel channel now marks; Goose Fair was held here until 1928.
Designed by Thomas Cecil Howitt and opened in 1929, on the site of the old Exchange at the head of the Old Market Square.

After large-scale slum clearance, the Broad Marsh shopping centre was officially opened on 25 March 1975. It closed in 2020 and was left partially demolished; caves found beneath it, dug into the soft sandstone, became part of the City of Caves.
A Georgian town house built in 1752. The Nottingham Subscription Library, founded in 1816, moved in during 1821.
The medieval castle was demolished after the Civil War and a ducal mansion built on the rock. Rioters burnt the mansion in 1831; it reopened as a museum in 1878.
The building began in 1839 as a grand Wesleyan chapel on Broad Street. Broadway opened here in 1990, and one of its screens is the only cinema screen designed by Sir Paul Smith.
Opened in 1865 and designed by Charles J. Phipps.
The building opened in 1876 as the Alexandra Skating Rink. Rock City opened in December 1980, with the Undertones playing the first gig, and holds 2,000 people.
Built in 1877 to designs credited to Edwin Hill, it is one of the few surviving Victorian music halls, under a high arched glass roof on laminated wooden arches.
Built as a Methodist mission hall and opened in 1909.
A modernist theatre designed by Peter Moro, opened in 1963.
A concert hall built next to the Theatre Royal and opened in 1982.
An art centre designed by Caruso St John and opened in 2009, its walls patterned with lace.

Wilford stayed a village until the later 19th century. With woods around it and riverside amenities such as the Ferry Inn, it attracted many visitors from Nottingham. The Notts County goalkeeper Albert Iremonger was its landlord until his death in 1958.
Opened in 1870, replacing a ferry that had crossed here for some 400 years. Pedestrians paid a halfpenny toll. It was closed to traffic in 1974.
A footbridge built by the city's water department, mainly to carry water pipes across the Trent to the reservoir on Wilford Hill. The engineer was Arthur Brown.

The church dates from the late 14th century and is thought to have been founded by Gervase de Wilford in around 1361. Inside are two memorials to the poet Henry Kirke White, who drew much inspiration from Wilford and Clifton.
Thomas Forman, who founded the Nottingham Post, bought Wilford House from the Smith family after the newspaper's successful launch.
Jeremiah Brandreth, born in Wilford, led the Pentrich rising of 1817 and was known as the Nottingham Captain. He was hanged for high treason outside Derby Gaol that November, and then beheaded.
Captain John Deane, a former mercenary who had served in the Russian navy, retired to Wilford.
A coal-fired power station on the north bank of the Trent, opened in 1925. It closed in 1981 and was soon demolished; the Riverside Retail Park stands on its site.

The settlement began in the early 10th century, when defences and houses were built at the south end of Trent Bridge to guard Nottingham against the Danes. Domesday, in 1086, records it as part of the manor of Clifton.
The first recorded match was played on ground behind the Trent Bridge Inn in 1838, and William Clarke opened the ground in 1841. It hosted its first Test match, England against Australia, in 1899.

Nottingham Forest moved here in 1898, to their seventh home. The name dates from 1897, when Nottingham was granted city status, and Notts County's Meadow Lane is only three hundred yards away, on the other side of the Trent.
The first Test at Trent Bridge, England against Australia in June 1899, was W. G. Grace's last Test and Wilfred Rhodes's first.

src.title: Australian cricket team in England in 1899

links.text: Nottinghamshire County Council's headquarters, designed by Vincent Harris. Building paused during the Second World War, and it was only completed in 1954.
The cricketer William Clarke married Mary Chapman, the inn's landlady, and the Trent Bridge cricket ground began in a field behind the pub.

The Musters family gained the West Bridgford estate in 1523, reputedly by winning it in a game of cards. When they sold land for building they set strict rules for it, and the village grew into a suburb, with its own council from 1894 and part of the borough of Rushcliffe from 1972.
A medieval church of which little remains. Thomas Chambers Hine restored it in 1872, and in 1896 a new nave and chancel were begun, their foundation stone laid by Lady Byron of Thrumpton Hall.
In 1941 a German bomber dropped a line of bombs across Lady Bay. New houses went up on the bomb sites in the 1950s and 1960s, and Pinders Ponds, to the east, are thought to be flooded bomb craters.

In 1964 an American company opened what was called the UK's first major out-of-town superstore on Loughborough Road. In 1966 the young Asda chain took it over, and in 1999 replaced it with a much larger store on the land next to it.
The Midland Railway built this bridge for its direct line to Melton Mowbray and London. The line closed in 1969, and in 1979 the bridge was turned over to road traffic.
A church dating from the 12th century, listed Grade II*. Arthur Brewill and Basil Baily rebuilt its chancel in 1894, and its east window has glass by Morris & Co.

src.title: Church of the Holy Rood, Edwalton

links.text: The station opened in 1880 on the Midland Railway's direct line from Nottingham to Melton Mowbray, which let its London expresses avoid Leicester. It closed to passengers in 1941, and its site is now housing. Beyond it the line became the Old Dalby test track, where the Advanced Passenger Train was tried.
A district built mostly in the 1990s, named after a garden in Poole. Its tram, opened in 2015, runs along a disused railway line.
The iron bridge was designed by Marriott Ogle Tarbotton and built between 1868 and 1871. A medieval bridge of more than 20 stone arches, begun in 1156, crossed the river nearby.

A mile and a quarter of flood defences along the Trent, built between 1898 and 1901 under the borough engineer Arthur Brown. Part of it was later laid out as Memorial Gardens to the dead of the First World War.
Notts County moved here on 3 September 1910. Divided by the Trent, Meadow Lane and the City Ground are the closest pair of football grounds in England.
Much of the Meadows' pre-1919 terraced housing was demolished to make way for a new development of modern council housing, and the viaduct carrying the Great Central railway came down in 1975.
Designed by the City Engineer Thomas Wallis Gordon, on land beside the Trent given by Sir Jesse Boot, and unveiled on 11 November 1927. It remembers the men of Nottingham who died in both World Wars.
For 700 years the Clifton family owned the manor of Clifton, and Clifton Hall was their manor house.
The Nottingham poet Henry Kirke White, a butcher's son, published Clifton Grove, a Sketch in Verse, in 1803, aged 17. He died in 1806, aged 21.
A medieval church, listed Grade I. Lewis Nockalls Cottingham restored it in 1846, and much of the decoration is by George Frederick Bodley.
Planned from 1950, the Clifton council estate was at one time the largest council estate in Europe. Since the 1980s most of its houses have passed into private ownership.
Opened in 1958 to take traffic off Trent Bridge, it was then the longest pre-stressed concrete bridge in the country. A second bridge beside it, opened in 1972, made the crossing a dual carriageway.
A tower mill built shortly after 1807 by the baker George Green. It burned in 1947, was restored and reopened in 1986, and is now part of a science centre.
William Booth, who founded the Salvation Army, was born in Sneinton on 10 April 1829. At 13 he was apprenticed to a pawnbroker. His birthplace is now a museum.
The present church was designed by Thomas Rickman and dates from 1837. It was extended between 1909 and 1912 to designs by George Frederick Bodley.
In the 1930s the city's wholesale fruit and vegetable market moved here from the Old Market Square.
A long passage to the bottom of the castle rock is known as Mortimer's Hole. In October 1330 Edward III's men came in by a secret tunnel, and Roger Mortimer was led out bound and gagged.

Caves under the old town, used over the years as a tannery, pub cellars and an air raid shelter. Two caves opening onto the cliff face held the only known underground tannery in Britain, set up in 1500.
Cave dwellings dug into the sandstone ridge extended out into Sneinton, where they were known as the Hermitage. What little remains can still be seen along Sneinton Hermitage.

Built from 1940 to fill and store ammunition, the depot was closed in 1983. Its land is now a transport heritage centre, a business park and Rushcliffe Country Park.
In 1941 a German bomber dropped a line of bombs across Lady Bay. New houses went up on the bomb sites in the 1950s and 1960s, and Pinders Ponds, to the east, are thought to be flooded bomb craters.

The church dates from the late 14th century and is thought to have been founded by Gervase de Wilford in around 1361. Inside are two memorials to the poet Henry Kirke White, who drew much inspiration from Wilford and Clifton.
The Nottingham poet Henry Kirke White, a butcher's son, published Clifton Grove, a Sketch in Verse, in 1803, aged 17. He died in 1806, aged 21.
An art centre designed by Caruso St John and opened in 2009, its walls patterned with lace.
A medieval church of which little remains. Thomas Chambers Hine restored it in 1872, and in 1896 a new nave and chancel were begun, their foundation stone laid by Lady Byron of Thrumpton Hall.
A medieval church, listed Grade I. Lewis Nockalls Cottingham restored it in 1846, and much of the decoration is by George Frederick Bodley.

Built in 1881–1884 to pump drinking water for Nottingham from deep wells, with two beam engines by James Watt & Co. and an engine house by Marriott Ogle Tarbotton, ornate with cast iron and stained glass. It pumped until 1969 and opened as a museum in 1976.

John Leavers lived here, at Canning Circus, where a plaque calls him the inventor of the Leavers lace machine, in 1813. He improved John Heathcoat's lace machine, and in 1821 emigrated to Grand-Couronne in Normandy.

The first recorded match was played on ground behind the Trent Bridge Inn in 1838, and William Clarke opened the ground in 1841. It hosted its first Test match, England against Australia, in 1899.
The cricketer William Clarke married Mary Chapman, the inn's landlady, and the Trent Bridge cricket ground began in a field behind the pub.

John Hutchinson, born at Owthorpe in 1615, held Nottingham Castle for Parliament from 1643 and signed Charles I's death warrant. He died a prisoner in 1664 and is buried at Owthorpe; his wife Lucy's Memoirs of his life made him famous.
